--- title: "Twenty years of northern border crossings" subtitle: "Seasonality, the 2020 collapse, and which ports actually came back" date: last-modified author: "Jacob Gray" categories: [SQL, Python, Power BI, Logistics] draft: true --- ::: {.finding-box} [The headline. Something like: truck volumes at [port] recovered to [X]% of 2019 by [year] while passenger crossings reached only [Y]%, and the divergence shows up months before [the policy change] rather than after it.] ::: ## The question Crossing volume drives everything downstream in a border brokerage — staffing, clearance lead time, where a delay is about to happen. The data is public and goes back to 1996, which is long enough to separate normal seasonality from an actual shift. ## The data ::: {.provenance}
Source
Border Crossing/Entry Data, Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
Coverage
Monthly counts by port, measure (trucks, loaded containers, personal vehicles, pedestrians, rail), 1996–present.
Retrieved
[Date]
Known limits
Counts inbound crossings only, not outbound, and counts conveyances rather than shipment value. A truck is a truck whether it is full or empty.
::: ## Approach [Replace with what you did:] - Load to SQLite; the file is long-format and clean enough to query directly. - Index monthly volumes to a 2019 baseline per port so ports of different sizes are comparable. - Decompose one port series into trend and seasonal components to show the size of the normal summer peak against the 2020 break. - Compare Blaine, Sumas, and Lynden against the northern border as a whole. ```{sql} #| eval: false select port_name, strftime('%Y', date) as yr, sum(value) filter (where measure = 'Trucks') as trucks from crossings where border = 'US-Canada Border' and state = 'Washington' group by port_name, yr order by port_name, yr; ``` ## What I found [Two charts at most. One long time series with the seasonal shape visible, one recovery comparison indexed to 2019. Write a sentence under each.] [This is where you add what the data does not show — the operational reason a port behaves the way it does. That context is your advantage.] ## What I would do differently [Candidates: conveyance counts are a poor proxy for trade value, so joining Census district-level trade data would show whether fewer trucks carried more value; and a proper interrupted time series would test the 2020 break rather than describing it.] --- *Code for this project: [GitHub](https://github.com/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/REPO).*
